summary: Initial migration discovery: Sapphire is evaluating moving from OpenAI managed + vLLM in-house serving to Redwood Hosted or Dedicated, with an eye on private deployment later. Key concerns: latency parity with current vLLM setup, quantization/compatibility with TGI models, SOC2/KMS requirements, and a clear SLA for bursty e-commerce traffic. Agreed to run benchmarks and exchange security docs.
topics: dedicated vs hosted vs private timeline
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2028-03-08 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Emily (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Mark (Sapphire CTO), Lena (Sapphire ML Lead), Omar (Sapphire SecOps)

[00:00] Emily: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll just do intros quick. I'm Emily, I'm the account lead at Redwood.
[00:06] Mark: Hey, Mark, CTO at Sapphire. Thanks.
[00:08] Lena: Lena, ML lead.
[00:10] Omar: Omar, SecOps.
[00:12] Samir: And I'm Samir, I'm on the solutions engineering side, I focus on migration and benchmarks.

[00:20] Emily: Nice. Quick agenda - understand your current stack, blockers, security needs, and agree next steps. Mark, can you give us the high level of what you run today?
[00:30] Mark: Sure. We run OpenAI for most of the prod generation, but for latency-sensitive flows - checkout, personalization - we've built an in-house v-l-l-m cluster running TGI-backed models, quantized to 4-bit. That gives us sub-50ms token latencies for short prompts. The problem is operational cost and maintenance, and we're trying to simplify.
[00:55] Lena: Yeah and we need eval parity - our A/B tests versus OpenAI are tuned to the v-l-l-m outputs so we want to keep scoring consistent.
[01:08] Omar: Security wise, we need SOC two, SSO (S A M L), KMS for key management, and audit logs tied to our SIEM.
[01:20] Emily: Great, that helps. Samir, quick reaction on the vllm/TGI part?
[01:26] Samir: So, first, we see this a lot. The two main questions: 1) Can Redwood match the latency characteristics of an in-house vllm/tgi pipeline when you need sub-50ms tokens, and 2) can we reproduce your eval parity when switching model variants or quantization? The short answer is yes, but with caveats.
[01:45] Mark: Caveats?
[01:47] Samir: You have to pick the right deployment mode. Hosted can be tuned - we have low-latency multi-tenant pools, but for the absolute lowest jitter and token p99 you typically go Dedicated or Private. Also kernel selection and KV cache behavior matters - we've done optimizations similar to what v-l-l-m does but we need to measure with your prompt distributions.
[02:10] Lena: When you say KV cache, are you talking about prefix caching per session? We rely heavily on reuse across sessions.
[02:16] Samir: Yeah, prefix/KV cache. We have automatic caching for repeated prefixes and we expose knobs to tune TTL and shard affinity. That often recovers a lot of the latency you see on short chats.
[02:30] Mark: What about quantization? Our TGI setup uses 4-bit GPTQ-style quant, and we tuned it end-to-end. Will Redwood accept a quantized model artifact or do you require conversion?
[02:42] Samir: For Dedicated and Private, customers can bring quantized artifacts. For Hosted, we have curated model variants and some limited support for customer artifacts via an upload process, but there are constraints on custom kernels. We often recommend doing an evaluation where you give us a sample quantized model or replicate it with our quant profiles so we can benchmark parity.
[03:00] Emily: Also to call out, we have model variants and a compatibility matrix for TGI and vllm builds we've validated. I can share that doc after the call.
[03:09] Mark: Perfect.

[03:20] --- 5 minute mark summary/quick notes in transcript omitted ---

[03:30] Lena: There's also the inference cost angle — dedicated hardware seemed cheaper per token when we were at scale, but we also have unpredictable spikes during sales.
[03:40] Samir: That's exactly what Dedicated is for - you get predictable throughput and reserved capacity, and we offer burst policies for short peaks into a shared pool. You can choose commit levels, and we model the unit cost so you can compare to your current spend.
[03:55] Mark: How are the fallbacks handled if the Dedicated pool is saturated? We can't have checkout traffic go down.
[04:01] Samir: We have automated fallback policies - you can route to a cheaper hosted variant or to a smaller but compatible model. You can also set region-level routing and prioritize critical routes. For checkout, most customers set a strict SLA and use canary capacity for that route.

[04:20] Omar: On the security front, you mentioned hosted has some constraints for uploads. We need to keep keys in our KMS and ensure no plaintext model artifacts leave our VPC. How does Private handle that?
[04:34] Samir: Private is customer-managed control plane — the models and keys stay inside your VPC or on-prem. We can integrate with your KMS/HSM via standard APIs. Private also gives you longer log retention and more granular RBAC. It is the usual path for regulated customers.
[04:50] Omar: Do you support bring-your-own-HSM?
[04:52] Samir: Yes, for Private we do; for Dedicated we can do customer KMS integrations and limited HSM options depending on the cloud.

[05:05] Mark: Let's talk about eval parity. Lena, we need the same eval scores within a small delta. How do you approach regression testing?
[05:13] Lena: Right. Our thresholds are fairly tight — BLEU-ish and embedding cosine deltas and downstream task metric drift under 2%.
[05:22] Samir: We have Eval pipelines and a 'redwood-eval' harness. For migrations we run side-by-side comparisons with the same prompt set, random seeds, and temperature controls. We also track log-prob deltas and repeatability. We will run your test suite during the pilot.
[05:38] Mark: Are there gotchas with RNG or tokenizer differences between TGI and Redwood runtime?
[05:44] Samir: Tokenizers can differ — token offsets especially if you're using byte-level tokenizers or custom merges. RNG seeding should be deterministic if you control seeds and the runtime supports it; sometimes GPUs/quantization change low-level numerics so tiny diffs occur. We surface those in the eval report.

[06:05] Emily: For timeline, what's your target?
[06:09] Mark: Ideally we want to be piloting in two weeks and potentially switch to Dedicated in 6-8 weeks if the numbers look good. But security signoff might push that.
[06:19] Emily: Okay, that's doable. We'll propose a pilot plan: 2-week focused benchmark using Dedicated trial capacity, run your evals, and produce a regression report.

[06:30] Lena: On the technical checklist, we need to validate: tokenizer parity, quantized weights load, KV cache performance, latency p50/p95/p99, and cost modeling.
[06:42] Samir: We'll instrument with per-token breakdown and provide a latency/cost dashboard. We can also run an end-to-end checkout flow to measure tail latencies.

[07:00] Mark: Any limitations on sequence lengths? Our models sometimes use 8k windows for long context.
[07:05] Samir: We support up to 32k in Dedicated/Private with tuned kernel selection. Hosted has quotas but can handle higher lengths with configuration. For long context, cache management and memory planning matter; we will estimate GPU footprint during the bench.

[07:30] Omar: Compliance questions — do you publish your SOC two and ISO attachments? We need the report and the pen test summary.
[07:38] Emily: Yes, we can share our SOC 2 Type II and the recent pen test summary under an NDA. I'll attach them in the follow-up.
[07:46] Omar: Also, we need to ensure audit logs correlate to our SIEM events and support SAML assertion mapping for user IDs.
[07:55] Samir: We emit structured audit logs and can ship to S3 or directly to your SIEM. SAML mapping is supported for the Console, and we have RBAC controls per token/route.

[08:10] --- Minor crosstalk about calendar invites and doc links ---

[08:25] Lena: For the pilot, do you need all the model artifacts or can you run against the endpoints?
[08:30] Samir: Ideally both. If you can provide quantized artifacts we can run inference locally in Dedicated/Private to verify bit-exact behavior. If that's not possible, we replicate the quantization profile and run side-by-side tests against your endpoint.

[08:50] Mark: Is there a risk that model conversion will change outputs significantly?
[08:54] Samir: There's always risk. That's why we compare log-probs and downstream metrics. Sometimes a conversion introduces small deg tradeoffs but we work to stay within your thresholds.

[09:10] Emily: Any procurement or legal constraints we should be aware of?
[09:14] Mark: We have standard vendor terms plus a requirement for data residency in eu-west-1 for production. Also need a 99.9% SLA for checkout route.
[09:26] Emily: We can do region pinning and Dedicated with SLA; we'll flag the SLA requirement for the renewals/legal team.

[09:40] Omar: One more — do you support model registry integrations? Our MLOps uses an internal registry and CI pipelines.
[09:47] Samir: Yes, we integrate with common registries; for Private you can mount registries or use a pull model. We also have a deployment API so CI can call and trigger rollouts.

[10:00] --- Midpoint, quick clarifying questions ---

[10:12] Lena: Metrics — do you provide token-level cost at route level? We need to show business stakeholders the cost per checkout.
[10:20] Samir: Yes, Redwood Console has per-route token/latency breakdowns with attribution by model and token type. We can export CSVs for finance.

[10:32] Mark: Demo request — can Samir show a short run of the bench runner?
[10:36] Samir: Sure, I can share a quick screen or repo after the call, but for today I'll walk through the steps. First, we take your prompt corpus, sample based on production distribution, run in parallel on your vllm endpoint and our trial Dedicated instance, capture tokens, latency, log-probs, and embed deltas, then produce a diff.

[10:58] Lena: That sounds right. We have a billing spike pattern from promotions where traffic triples for ~10 minutes - can the Dedicated plan burst?
[11:05] Samir: Yes, burst capacity can be configured as guaranteed vs best-effort. For mission-critical routes you can set a hard SLA and we keep warm capacity. There is a cost for reserved warm capacity but it's much cheaper than overprovisioning always.

[11:25] Mark: Anything else we need to prepare?
[11:29] Samir: Provide the eval set, a sample of production logs for distribution, and any quantized artifacts. If you can share a representative checkout request trace that includes prompt length distribution that'd be ideal.

[11:40] Emily: Okay, recap and next steps. We'll: 1) Send security pack (SOC 2 + pen test) by 2028-03-10; 2) Samir will prepare benchmark plan and cost/latency spreadsheet and deliver by 2028-03-13; 3) Mark will share prompt set by 2028-03-09; 4) We'll schedule pilot week of 2028-03-14. Anything to add?
[11:58] Mark: No, that covers it. Quick question — pricing cadence, do you invoice monthly or annual for Dedicated?
[12:06] Emily: We do both. Dedicated is usually monthly commits with annual discounts possible. I'll include pricing scenarios in the follow-up.

[12:20] Omar: One small operational note — our security team will want an architecture diagram for the Private option showing network flow and HSM boundaries.
[12:30] Samir: We'll include a diagram in the security pack.

[12:40] --- Closing small talk ---

[12:50] Emily: Thanks everyone, I'll follow up with the docs and schedule.
[12:54] Mark: Thanks.
[12:55] Lena: Thanks all.
[12:56] Omar: Bye.

[13:00] End of recording.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcript had some mis-heard acronyms (v-l-l-m appearing as 'vellum' in one spot, 'SOC 2' transcribed as 'sock two' briefly), and occasional speaker mis-attribution during cross talk.
